subject: hoverbike
pitch:
Category: Vehicle.
Subject: desert hoverbike.
Style: Star Wars.
reasoning:
I'm designing a desert hoverbike inspired by Star Wars speeder bikes, planning it as a static vehicle model without a joint rig since no creature animation is needed, aiming for a reasonably sized, well-structured TypeScript module.

Now I'm sketching the build plan: a tapered fuselage lofted from rear to nose roughly 2.6m long, resting on small landing skids near ground level with hover pads for slight clearance, using panelled and metal kit pieces for the hull and engine, glow elements for headlamp and instrument lighting, and a weathered sand-white paint scheme with rust-orange accents.

I'm fleshing out the speeder-bike details: twin rear engine nacelles with intake cones, upward-curving stabilizer fins, a saddle seat and handlebars, small windscreen, canards, side cargo pods, and a bedroll strapped to the back, plus smaller touches like a glowing headlamp and instrument screen, rivet detailing, made-up alien-script decals, a tattered pennant, hanging goggles, a canteen, and dust/weathering effects.

Since this is a static vehicle prop rather than a creature, I'm deciding no skeleton or joints are needed — just building the fuselage directly with the loft helper, defining stations along the body from tail to nose with position, width, and height values, and mirroring side details like the fins and cargo pods across the central axis. I'm laying out the main coordinate scheme with z as the forward axis, placing the rear around z=-1.3 and the nose tip around z=1.4.

Now I'm working out the hull paint, layering a base sand-white color with an orange racing stripe along the top centerline, dirt staining near the lower surfaces using a smoothstep blend, subtle noise for weathering, and a panelled texture overlay to suggest hull plating.

For the engines, I'm placing twin rear cylinders using swept rods with metal coloring, plus lathe-built intake cones at the front and nozzle shapes at the rear.

Placing engine nacelles forward of the fuselage, extending from around z=-1.5 to 0.55 with a conical intake tip reaching to z=0.95, with the cone's tip oriented along +z for the forward-pointing spinner look.

Still defining fin geometry...

Working out the canard extrusion direction and outline shape, then I'll move on to building the cockpit seat as a cushioned box on top of the body.

For the saddle I'll use a brown leather-colored pad with stitching, add small footrest plates with grip stripes near the sides, and a sloped dashboard console with a glowing screen decal in front of the seat. For the windscreen I'm planning a tinted blue-cyan glass slab using a swept trapezoid shape, kept as flat opaque color rather than true transparency.

Now I'm working out the handlebars as a curved sweep between the grips through the stem, with rubber grip capsules, brass end caps, and small brake levers. I'm also placing a headlamp housing at the nose using a lathe shape oriented forward, plus smaller accent lights beside the console.

For the underside, I'm adding four hover pads as lathe bowls with glowing cyan discs facing downward, positioned near the front and rear of the body, with thin folding landing struts extending down from the pads to the ground.

Switching approach to simpler skid runners: two curved rods running along the length of the craft, swept up slightly at the front, touching the ground near y=0, connected to the body by short struts.

For the exhaust, I'm lathing a flared bell nozzle at the rear engine with a glowing cyan disc inside, and adding a bedroll accessory strapped across the top rear of the body with tan cloth and a painted stripe.

I'm also figuring out strap rings using slightly oversized short cylinders oriented along x, plus considering a canteen pair and a satchel box hanging off the hull near the engines for added detail.

Now I'm adding a tattered cloth pennant streaming from the left fin tip, built as a thin extruded shape with rope tails, plus goggles hanging off the left handlebar using tori and amber lens discs. I'm also planning a decal strip with glyph-like markings on the hull side for extra texture.

Working out the orientation math, I confirm text direction doesn't matter much since the glyphs are decorative and unreadable anyway. I could instead just add a simple stylized number decal on the side, like a racing plate.

Now I'm planning the instrument console with a tilted screen plane that'll glow, positioning it on a slanted box part for the dashboard look.

For the screen texture, I'm sketching a radar-style SVG with a dark teal background, green sweep circle, data bars, and a red warning blip. Then I'm narrowing down the texture set to roughly 5-8 items: glyphs, screen, plate numbers, an emblem (sun and wings, scavenger-style), hazard warning chevrons for the engines, and possibly a pennant pattern — keeping the list lean rather than overloading it.

For paints and materials, I'm planning hull and dirt lighting, metal finishes for the engines (iron, steel paneling), copper piping with verdigris aging, leather grain, striped cloth, and rubber.

For the greebles, I'm adding copper rod piping between the engine and body, and rows of thin slat boxes near the engines to act as exhaust vents, roughly six per side. For the engine intakes, I'm considering a lathe-shelled hollow cone with a dark inner disc textured like a fan to suggest an intake ring, finished off with a bell-shaped lip.

Working out the intake geometry...

Adding more engine details...

I'll make a reusable dusty() helper that adds dust patches based on normal orientation and proximity to the ground. Then I'm planning the imports needed — builder, paint utilities, metal/panelled kits, maybe glow — while deciding to skip extras like gear details to keep things simple, and checking what the builder returns when there's no joint defined.

Setting up color palette and the paint function...

Still defining hull paint...

I'm lofting the fuselage shape using the hull paint material, then thinking about adding a nose cone spike with a metallic tip color and a small lamp detail near the nose beak.

For the seat, I'm positioning a frustum box shape aligned to match the body's top height, giving it a leather grain texture, then adding a taller backrest piece behind it using another frustum box.

Now I'm working on the handlebar assembly: a steel stem rod rising from the body up to the bar mount, then a curved handlebar built from a series of points sweeping from the left grip forward and center to form the bar shape.

Adding a slim brake lever rod, then shaping the windscreen as an extruded outline tilted backward for a leaning profile, symmetric along the x-axis.

Working through the console's tilt rotation, I want the top face angled to point toward the rider rather than away, so I need a negative rotation around X of about 20 degrees to get the normal tilting correctly toward -z.

Now I'm checking heights against the hull geometry -- comparing where the console top sits relative to hull height at different z stations to make sure the console base aligns properly, and verifying the windscreen base height matches the hull top at that position too.

Since the windscreen floats slightly above the hull, I'm adding a small base mount box to close that gap, repositioning it and tilting it along its mounting direction. I'm also planning instrument glow via a screen texture and small side position lights, then thinking through footrest placement -- realizing the engine intake geometry on the sides would collide with footrests at the planned position, so I need to shift the engines to make room.

Finishing the engine details, I'm adding the fan disc and nozzle bell at the rear, checking the rider's seated leg positions fit within the hull. Now I'm planning pylons connecting the hull sides to the engines using angled steel rods plus panel plates, and starting on rear fins extruding off the engine sides.

Working out the fin geometry — a tall swept outline mounted on the engine's outer top, oriented to lean outward at a normalized angle. I'm checking that the fin's height brings the total vehicle height to roughly 1.22 units, which still seems reasonable compared to the handlebars.

Still writing fin paint logic...

I also want to add a small pennant extrusion near the fin's top rear edge, positioning it using the fin's local coordinate system so it attaches naturally to the geometry.

Finishing the swallowtail pennant polygon shape, confirming the points form a simple non-crossing outline, then adding a tattered red-brown cloth color and checking the orientation axes so the pennant sits correctly canted at the fin top.

Now I'm laying out the four hover pad positions under the hull bottom, each with a small lathe-built housing profile and a glowing disc cylinder on top.

Then I'm adding stubby rod struts connecting skids to the hull, deciding tapered skid rails make sense as simple landing gear even though hoverbikes don't strictly need them, and plotting the skid path points along the bottom with a slight upward taper near the front.

I notice the pads at x ±0.24 would collide with the skids at x .27, so I'm repositioning the pads inward to roughly ±0.12-0.13 near front and back to keep clearances clean, settling on four pads total. Now I'm working out the exhaust nozzle geometry as a lathe shape at the rear, defining its outline profile.

Adding an exhaust flame core with a short narrowing cone pointing outward, plus vent slat boxes along the top of the engines...

Now I'm adding engine rings as toruses sized to circumscribe the rod radius, and planning decal placement for glyphs, a nose emblem, and a number plate on the hull.

For the fin emblem, I'm figuring out the outward normal direction based on the fin's local axis so the decal projects correctly onto the thin surface.

I'm now considering placing the emblem on the hull's side too, but worried about plane geometry floating or penetrating the curved surface given the varying cross-section widths. I'll switch to using decal projection for the hull emblem instead, trusting it to snap correctly onto the surface.

Then I'm adding a tapered antenna whip rod extending from near the seat up past the fin height, and finishing with small cargo details like a bedroll and satchel.

I'll skip the tow cable coil but add goggles hanging off the right handlebar using torus lenses, then design a headlamp housing lathed near the nose top with a cylindrical lens.

I'm also planning small amber nav lights on fin tips, a red tail glow on the seat backrest, console corner accents, and a metal nose spike with small forward canards under it, while skipping any gun-like forms.

Checking overall proportions: nose spike extends total bike length to about 3.25m, fin tops reach roughly 1.1m, and antenna/handlebar heights stay under 1.35m -- all reasonable for the hoverbike's swoop silhouette. Now I'm writing helper functions for side pairs and direction vectors to set up the geometry placement.

I'm defining a cylinder helper that builds flat-shaded tube parts for the frame and fittings, then moving on to sketching the SVG textures: a dark dashboard screen with a green radar sweep, amber bar graph, and cyan speed readout, plus a faceted fan texture with nine rotated blade paths.

Now I'm planning glyph decals as a transparent strip of randomly generated orange script-like marks for hull detailing, and a number plate texture with a rounded cream rect, ink stroke border, and stenciled ID text like "R-77" alongside a hazard mark.

I'm placing the plate decal onto the cylindrical engine rod, orienting it along the rod's axis, and sizing/positioning it near the nacelle. I'll skip the hazard stripe and instead add a circular emblem with a sun-and-wings motif and bike chevron for a scavenger-faction look, plus consider which surfaces get glow (screen yes, fan no, pad flat colour) and where to apply pennant paint.

Now I'm adding small details like rivet bolts, copper exhaust pipe rails running along the engine tops with brackets, cloth wraps on the handlebar, a saddle skirt under the seat with stitched leather-grain paint, and a canteen cylinder hung near the bedroll on the hull's rear side.

Working out hull and engine widths at different z positions, I realize the gap is too narrow for the canteen there, so I'm relocating it onto the seat back or as a satchel box beside the backrest, and considering a crate mounted on the rear deck between the fins near the bedroll instead.

I'll place the canteen lying atop the bedroll with a strap, add loft stations for the hull, then finish with a rear heat shield plate, front bumper, and maybe under-nose canards.

Writing hull paint logic...

Writing glyph generator logic...

I'm finishing the meta export with the model's name and description, then building a lathe helper function with configurable segment count for faceted versus smooth shading, and positioning a circular fan disc near the intake lip.

I'm checking placement details for the fan disc and spinner cone relative to the lip and end cap radii, confirming the rod helper's argument order for position, radius, and color options, then starting the skid sweep using a Catmull curve.

Now I'm working out the torus orientation for the ring (axis along Z, aligned with the engine), setting up cylinder straps across the bedroll along the x-axis, and laying out Catmull points for a symmetric handlebar sweep from the right grip to the left grip, including the stem connection point.

Next I'm placing an antenna rod on the right fin with a glowing red tip sphere, positioning a small glowing taillight box on the rear of the backrest, and sizing a decal glyph strip for the body.

Now I'm adding footrests as boxes near the lower hull with support struts and grip ridge details, plus a painted console panel. I'm also considering adding small gauge dials using circular geometry textured like a clockwork face on the console.

Positioning two brass-bezeled gauges flanking the screen, calculating the tilted console top surface geometry to place them correctly relative to the sloped panel.
